title: Preface
summary: Apple Inc.’s Form 10-K cover page identifies its annual report for the fiscal year ended September 30, 2023, company details, SEC file number, California incorporation, headquarters, and contact information. It lists common stock and multiple notes registered on Nasdaq, with no Section 12(g) securities. Checkboxes report issuer status, filing and interactive-data compliance, filer classification, internal-control attestation, and shell-company status. It also gives nonaffiliate market value as of March 31, 2023, and common shares outstanding as of October 20, 2023.

title: DOCUMENTS INCORPORATED BY REFERENCE
summary: Apple’s 2023 Form 10-K incorporates portions of its 2024 proxy statement into Part III and provides its filing contents: business, risks, cybersecurity, legal matters, market and financial results, governance, compensation, exhibits, and related disclosures. It explains forward-looking-statement risks, terminology, fiscal-year conventions, and that “Apple” and “Company” include subsidiaries. The Business section describes Apple’s products and 52- or 53-week fiscal year: iPhone, Mac, iPad, wearables, home devices, and accessories, with their operating systems and product lines.

title: Apple Background, Products, and Forward-Looking Statements
summary: The page explains that Apple’s 2023 Form 10-K contains risk-bearing forward-looking statements, which are not guarantees, may differ from actual results, and generally will not be updated; it also defines fiscal-period references and “Company”/“Apple.” Apple designs, manufactures, and markets devices and services, with a fiscal year ending in September. Products include iPhone, Mac, iPad, wearables and headphones, home streaming and speaker devices, and Apple-branded and third-party accessories.

title: Services, Business Segments, and Distribution
key_items: Advertising; AppleCare; Cloud Services; Digital Content; Payment Services
summary: The page describes Apple’s advertising, AppleCare support and coverage, cross-device cloud services, digital content platforms and subscriptions, and payment services. It outlines its five geographic reportable segments and their territories, noting that each is managed separately to reflect customers, distribution partners, and regional market dynamics. Customers span consumer, business, education, enterprise, and government markets; sales use direct retail, online, and sales-force channels plus third-party intermediaries. In 2023, direct channels generated 37% of net sales and indirect channels 63%.

title: Competition
summary: The text outlines Apple’s intense competition, driven by pricing pressure, rapid innovation and imitation, and the need to deliver timely products, with success depending on features, quality, design, ecosystem, distribution, support and reputation. It describes component supply risks, including limited sources, shortages, price swings, custom-part capacity constraints and uncertain supply agreements. It notes ongoing R&D, licensing and acquisitions, and Apple’s broad global IP portfolio, filing efforts, reliance on employee expertise, use of third-party IP and uncertainty about future licenses.

title: Competition, Components, R&D, and Intellectual Property
summary: The Company’s competitiveness depends on timely innovation and product development amid intense competition, price pressure, imitation, and rivals with broader offerings and resources. Component supply is generally available from multiple sources but can face single-source dependence, shortages, price fluctuations, capacity constraints, and uncertain supply-agreement renewals. R&D, licensing, and acquisitions support new technologies and offerings. Intellectual property includes a broad global portfolio, though success also relies on employees; the Company continually seeks protection and may need third-party licenses whose future availability and terms are uncertain.

title: Business, Workforce, and Investor Information
key_items: Business Seasonality and Product Introductions; Available Information
Workplace Practices and Policies; Compensation and Benefits; Inclusion and Diversity; Engagement; Health and Safety
summary: The page describes seasonal sales patterns and how product launches and channel inventory affect sales and expenses. It outlines Apple’s workforce size and commitments to fair workplace practices, competitive compensation and benefits, inclusion and diversity, employee engagement, and health and safety. It also explains where investors can access SEC filings and company updates, noting website content is not incorporated into the filing.

title: Item 1A. Risk Factors
summary: The Company’s business, reputation, operating results, financial condition, and stock price may be adversely affected by known or unknown risks. Past performance is not a reliable guide to future results, and historical trends should not be used to predict them. The risk discussion contains forward-looking statements and should be read alongside the Form 10-K’s MD&A and consolidated financial statements and notes.

title: Macroeconomic and Industry Risks
key_items: The Company’s operations and performance depend significantly on global and regional economic conditions and adverse economic conditions can materially adversely affect the Company’s business, results of operations and financial condition.

The Company’s business can be impacted by political events, trade and other international disputes, war, terrorism, natural disasters, public health issues, industrial accidents and other business interruptions.
Global markets for the Company’s products and services are highly competitive and subject to rapid technological change, and the Company may be unable to compete effectively in these markets.
summary: The text outlines Apple’s exposure to global economic conditions: downturns, inflation, interest and currency changes can reduce demand, destabilize partners, and impair receivables, financing, liquidity and financial assets. Political and trade conflicts, tariffs, disasters, climate change, accidents, cyberattacks, labor issues and public-health crises may disrupt commerce, suppliers, manufacturing, logistics, sales and services; limited component sources worsen impacts, and insurance may not cover losses. It also describes intense competition, rapid technological change, price pressure, short product cycles and competitors’ resources, imitation and IP infringement. Apple’s success depends on costly R&D, innovation, effective IP protection and continual product and service improvements, with no assurance of adequate returns or competitiveness.

title: Business Risks

nodes.title: To remain competitive and stimulate customer demand, the Company must successfully manage frequent introductions and transitions of products and services.
nodes.summary: The Company’s competitiveness and customer demand depend on frequent successful product and service introductions, upgrades, and transitions in volatile, competitive markets. Success requires timely development and market acceptance; managing new-technology and production ramp-up risks; adequate application software; purchase commitments and inventory aligned with demand; sufficient product availability at expected costs; and avoiding quality defects or deficiencies. Future success is not assured.

nodes.title: The Company depends on component and product manufacturing and logistical services provided by outsourcing partners, many of which are located outside of the U.S.
nodes.summary: The Company relies on concentrated, often single-source overseas outsourcing partners for manufacturing, assembly, components, transportation and logistics. This lowers costs but limits control and creates risks involving quality, supply, responsiveness, labor and conduct violations, disruptions, and recovery of equipment or supplier prepayments. Limited sources, shortages, price volatility, supplier failures, custom-component constraints, and difficulty replacing or renewing suppliers can raise costs or delay products. Defects in hardware, software, components or services—including outages and safety issues—may cause customer harm, liability, recalls, expenses, reputational damage, reduced demand, and lost sales.

nodes.title: Supply Chain and Product Quality Risks
key_items: Future operating results depend upon the Company’s ability to obtain components in sufficient quantities on commercially reasonable terms.

The Company’s products and services may be affected from time to time by design and manufacturing defects that could materially adversely affect the Company’s business and result in harm to the Company’s reputation.
nodes.summary: Apple relies on geographically dispersed, often single-source suppliers and outsourcing partners; disruptions, financial distress, or logistics problems could restrict supply and impair equipment or prepayments. Shortages, price fluctuations, custom-component constraints, and difficulty renewing agreements or finding alternatives may harm results. Design, manufacturing, software, component, and service defects or outages may cause safety risks, liability, recalls, costs, customer dissatisfaction, reputational damage, reduced demand, and lost sales.

nodes.title: Inventory, Purchase Commitment, and IP Risks
key_items: The Company is exposed to the risk of write-downs on the value of its inventory and other assets, in addition to purchase commitment cancellation risk.
The Company relies on access to third-party intellectual property, which may not be available to the Company on commercially reasonable terms or at all.
nodes.summary: The Company may incur inventory and asset write-downs, impairment charges, and purchase commitment cancellation fees due to obsolescence, uncertain demand, and volatile markets that can lead to inaccurate forecasts or unused commitments. Its products and services also depend on third-party intellectual property licenses; potential infringement claims and inability to obtain licenses on reasonable terms could prevent sales or materially harm business and financial results.

nodes.title: The Company’s future performance depends in part on support from third-party software developers.
nodes.summary: The Company’s sales depend on third-party developers creating and maintaining appealing apps and services; its smaller market share may steer developers toward competitors, while rapid technological change can leave apps outdated or faulty. App Store regulatory, legal, competitive, and business changes could reduce sales or commissions and materially harm results. Digital-content licensing, availability, pricing, security requirements, and costly in-house production pose risks. Success also relies on retaining skilled employees and preserving an inclusive culture amid intense talent competition and changing workforce dynamics. The Company depends on carriers, wholesalers, retailers, resellers, and direct sales channels; carrier financing and subsidies may change or end.

nodes.title: App Store, Digital Content, and Talent Risks
key_items: Failure to obtain or create digital content that appeals to the Company’s customers, or to make such content available on commercially reasonable terms, could have a material adverse impact on the Company’s business, results of operations and financial condition.

The Company’s success depends largely on the talents and efforts of its team members, the continued service and availability of highly skilled employees, including key personnel, and the Company’s ability to nurture its distinctive and inclusive culture.
nodes.summary: App Store changes driven by competition, regulation, and litigation may reduce sales or commissions and materially harm results. Digital-content risks include losing or facing higher costs for third-party licenses, producing content that fails to attract customers, and being unable to provide required security technology affordably or promptly. Success also depends on retaining key and skilled employees amid intense competition and changing workforce dynamics, and sustaining an inclusive culture; failures could damage recruitment, operations, reputation, and financial performance.

nodes.title: The Company depends on the performance of carriers, wholesalers, retailers and other resellers.
nodes.summary: The Company relies on carriers, wholesalers, retailers and resellers, which also sell competitors’ offerings; it also sells directly. Carrier financing and subsidies may end, while reseller-support investments may not generate returns and resellers may weaken, stop selling its products or reduce orders and marketing. Complex IT systems and supply chains face outages and disruptions that may impede services, sales, manufacturing and shipping, harming business and reputation. Confidential-data breaches, including through suppliers and increasingly sophisticated attacks, may cause operational, financial, legal and reputational damage, litigation, investigations, fines, stock impacts and customer or commercial losses. Security controls, continuity plans and insurance may prove inadequate; protective measures such as encryption, authentication, monitoring and account freezes can themselves delay orders or restrict access.

nodes.title: Reseller Investment, IT Disruption, and Information Security Risks
key_items: The Company’s business and reputation are impacted by information technology system failures and network disruptions.

Losses or unauthorized access to or releases of confidential information, including personal information, could subject the Company to significant reputational, financial, legal and operational consequences.
nodes.summary: The Company’s reseller-support investments may not generate returns, and reseller weakness or uncertain demand could reduce product orders and marketing. IT failures and network disruptions—from varied hazards or cyber incidents—could disrupt online services, transactions, manufacturing, and shipping despite continuity measures. Confidential-data loss or unauthorized disclosure could cause reputational, financial, legal, and operational harm. Risks include attacks on the Company and third parties, which are frequent, increasingly sophisticated, and heightened by the Company’s profile; inadequate safeguards, phishing, customer-access restrictions, litigation, investigations, and insufficient insurance may compound losses.

nodes.title: Investment and Retail Operations Risks
key_items: Investment in new business strategies and acquisitions could disrupt the Company’s ongoing business, present risks not originally contemplated and materially adversely affect the Company’s business, reputation, results of operations and financial condition.
The Company’s retail stores are subject to numerous risks and uncertainties.
nodes.summary: Investments in new strategies and acquisitions may distract management, create unexpected costs and liabilities, face operational, regulatory, political or economic challenges, yield inadequate returns, require asset impairments or write-offs, and fail to deliver benefits—potentially harming the Company’s business, reputation, results and financial condition. Retail operations also face macroeconomic and general retail risks, as well as challenges controlling store construction and operating costs, managing retail partners and inventory-value fluctuations, and securing or renewing quality-location leases at reasonable costs.

summary: Business risks include dependence on frequent successful product launches, demand forecasting, inventory and purchase commitments, and third-party IP licenses; concentrated overseas suppliers and logistics partners, component shortages, cost volatility, defects, and supply disruptions; reliance on app developers, digital-content licenses, distribution channels, and carrier financing; App Store and regulatory changes; talent retention and inclusive culture; reseller investment; IT outages and cybersecurity or data breaches; and risks from acquisitions, new strategies, and retail operations, including costs, leases, and uncertain returns. These issues may disrupt operations, reduce sales, or cause liability, reputational damage, and financial losses.

title: Legal and Regulatory Compliance Risks
key_items: The Company’s business, results of operations and financial condition could be adversely impacted by unfavorable results of legal proceedings or government investigations.
The Company is subject to complex and changing laws and regulations worldwide, which exposes the Company to potential liabilities, increased costs and other adverse effects on the Company’s business.

Expectations relating to environmental, social and governance considerations and related reporting obligations expose the Company to potential liabilities, increased costs, reputational harm, and other adverse effects on the Company’s business.

The technology industry, including, in some instances, the Company, is subject to intense media, political and regulatory scrutiny, which exposes the Company to increasing regulation, government investigations, legal actions and penalties.
The Company’s business is subject to a variety of U.S. and international laws, rules, policies and other obligations regarding data protection.
summary: The text outlines Apple’s legal and regulatory risks: growing litigation, investigations, patent disputes and indemnity claims may be costly, disruptive, uninsured or lead to damages, injunctions, settlements, business changes and material losses. Complex, evolving global rules across numerous areas raise compliance costs and may restrict products, operations or imports. ESG commitments and reporting create investment, expectation, liability and reputational risks. Intense technology-sector scrutiny, antitrust actions, App Store regulation and investigations involving business partners may trigger fines, required changes and harm sales, competition, privacy perceptions and reputation. Worldwide privacy and data-protection laws impose changing obligations and penalties, including heightened requirements for sensitive health, financial, biometric and payment-card data; violations may cause investigations, litigation, fines, audits, higher costs or loss of payment processing. Management reported no other reasonably possible material contingency losses beyond specified disclosures.

title: Financial Risks
key_items: The Company expects its quarterly net sales and results of operations to fluctuate.
The Company’s financial performance is subject to risks associated with changes in the value of the U.S. dollar relative to local currencies.
The Company is exposed to credit risk and fluctuations in the values of its investment portfolio.

The Company is exposed to credit risk on its trade accounts receivable, vendor non-trade receivables and prepayments related to long-term supply agreements, and this risk is heightened during periods when economic conditions worsen.
The Company is subject to changes in tax rates, the adoption of new U.S. or international tax legislation and exposure to additional tax liabilities.
summary: The filing describes risks from quarterly sales and earnings volatility, varying and pressured margins, seasonality, product concentration, launches and operational disruptions; foreign-exchange movements and potentially ineffective hedges; investment-value and counterparty credit risks involving receivables, vendors and supply prepayments; and changing tax laws, rates, interpretations and audit outcomes. General risks include volatile share prices tied to expectations for growth, dividends and buybacks, potentially affecting investor confidence and employee retention. Unresolved staff comments: none; cybersecurity: not applicable.

title: Financial, Tax, Stock, and Cybersecurity Risks
key_items: The price of the Company’s stock is subject to volatility.
Item 1B. Unresolved Staff Comments; Item 1C. Cybersecurity
summary: The page discusses credit risks from unsecured, concentrated receivables and supply-agreement prepayments, especially during economic downturns, and tax risks from changing laws, rates, interpretations, and audits that could increase liabilities. It describes stock-price volatility and the potential effects of unmet expectations for growth, dividends, and repurchases. Unresolved staff comments are listed as none; cybersecurity is not applicable.

title: Properties and Legal Proceedings
key_items: Epic Games; Masimo; Other Legal Proceedings
summary: Apple’s Cupertino headquarters and facilities worldwide support corporate, R&D, data-center, retail, and other functions; the company considers them suitable and in good condition. Legal updates cover Epic’s App Store antitrust case, including an injunction, appeals, and a stay pending Supreme Court review; Masimo’s blood-oxygen patent dispute and an exclusion order expected to take effect December 25, 2023, which Apple plans to appeal; and other ordinary-course proceedings, some settled without material impact, whose uncertain outcomes could adversely affect results.

title: Item 4. Mine Safety Disclosures
summary: Mine safety disclosures are not applicable. Apple’s common stock trades on Nasdaq as AAPL, with 23,763 shareholders of record as of October 20, 2023. The filing reports quarterly share repurchases through September 30, 2023, including open-market, privately negotiated, and August accelerated share repurchases (ASRs), with share counts, average prices, and remaining authorization. Apple had a $90 billion May 2023 program, of which $15.9 billion was used; it used the prior program’s final $4.6 billion in the fourth quarter. Repurchases are discretionary and may use Rule 10b5-1 plans. August ASRs involved $5 billion in upfront payments, with final shares and average prices based on trading prices through the first quarter of 2024.

title: Stock Listing, Shareholders, and Repurchases
key_items: Item 5. Market for Registrant’s Common Equity, Related Stockholder Matters and Issuer Purchases of Equity Securities
Purchases of Equity Securities by the Issuer and Affiliated Purchasers
summary: Apple’s common stock trades on Nasdaq under AAPL, and it had 23,763 shareholders of record as of October 20, 2023. The page reports quarterly repurchases by period, including shares bought, average prices, and purchases under announced programs. It describes the $90 billion May 2023 authorization, amounts used and remaining, the prior program’s completion, and the programs’ nonbinding nature and permitted transaction methods. It also explains August accelerated share repurchase agreements totaling $5 billion, with final share delivery and average price based on trading prices through the first quarter of 2024.

title: Stock Performance and Reserved Item 6
summary: A five-year, dividend-reinvested total shareholder return comparison tracks Apple, the S&P 500, and the Dow Jones U.S. Technology Supersector Index, assuming $100 invested at September 28, 2018. Values are shown through September 2023; past performance does not predict future results. Item 6 is reserved.

title: MD&A Scope and Fiscal Period
key_items: Item 7. Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations
summary: The MD&A should be read with the consolidated financial statements and notes in Part II, Item 8. It covers 2023 and 2022 results and comparisons; 2021 information and 2022–2021 comparisons appear in the prior annual report. The fiscal year ends on the last Saturday of September and lasts 52 or 53 weeks. An extra week is added to the first quarter every five or six years to align quarters with calendar quarters; this occurred in 2023. Fiscal 2023 had 53 weeks, while 2022 and 2021 had 52.

title: Fiscal Year Highlights

nodes.title: Macroeconomic Conditions
nodes.summary: Apple reported 2023 net sales of $383.3 billion and net income of $97.0 billion; sales fell 3% ($11.0 billion), mainly due to currency weakness, lower Mac and iPhone sales, and partially offsetting Services growth. The text lists quarterly product, service, and software launches, including iPads, Macs, HomePod, Apple Vision Pro, operating-system updates, iPhone 15 models, and Apple Watch models. Apple authorized up to $90 billion in buybacks, raised its dividend to $0.24 per share, repurchased $76.6 billion of stock, and paid $15.0 billion in dividends. It notes risks from inflation, interest rates, and currencies. Segment sales and trends are reported: Americas −4%, Europe −1%, Greater China −2%, Japan −7%, and Rest of Asia Pacific +1%, with regional currency effects and product-category drivers described.

nodes.title: 2023 Segment Net Sales and Regional Performance
nodes.summary: The page presents net sales by reportable segment for 2023, 2022 and 2021. In 2023, Americas sales fell 4%, mainly due to lower iPhone and Mac sales, partly offset by Services. Europe fell 1%; currency weakness more than explained the decline, with lower Mac and Wearables, Home and Accessories sales partly offset by iPhone and Services. Greater China fell 2%, with currency weakness more than explaining the decline and lower Mac and iPhone sales. Japan fell 7%, with yen weakness more than explaining the drop and lower iPhone, Wearables, Home and Accessories, and Mac sales. Rest of Asia Pacific rose 1% despite unfavorable currency effects, as higher iPhone and Services sales outweighed lower Mac and iPad sales.

nodes.title: Rest of Asia Pacific
nodes.summary: The text reports Apple’s 2023 net sales by region and product/service category, with 2022 and 2021 comparisons. Regional sales fell in the Americas (4%), Europe (1%), Greater China (2%), and Japan (7%), while Rest of Asia Pacific rose 1%; currency weakness affected all regions except the Americas, with product-specific increases and declines detailed. By category, iPhone fell 2%, Mac 27%, iPad 3%, and Wearables, Home and Accessories 3%, while Services rose 9%. It explains the main drivers of each change and notes that product and Services sales include amortization of deferred values for bundled software upgrades and services.

nodes.title: Apple 2023 Net Sales by Category
nodes.summary: The page presents Apple net sales by category for 2021–2023 and explains that product sales include amortized value of bundled software upgrades, while Services includes amortized bundled services. In 2023 versus 2022, iPhone sales fell 2% ($4.9 billion), as lower non-Pro sales partly offset higher Pro sales; Mac fell 27% ($10.8 billion), mainly from laptops; iPad fell 3% ($1.0 billion), mainly from iPad mini and Air, partly offset by 9th- and 10th-generation models; and Wearables, Home and Accessories fell 3% ($1.4 billion), mainly from Wearables and Accessories. Services rose 9% ($7.1 billion), with growth across all business lines.

nodes.title: Services
nodes.summary: The text reports Apple’s 2023–2021 net sales by category, noting that 2023 iPhone sales fell 2% ($4.9 billion) as non-Pro declines outweighed Pro growth; Mac fell 27% ($10.8 billion), mainly from laptops; iPad fell 3% ($1.0 billion), mainly from mini and Air declines; Wearables, Home and Accessories fell 3% ($1.4 billion); and Services rose 9% ($7.1 billion) across all business lines. Product and Services sales include amortization of deferred values for bundled software upgrades and services, respectively. It presents gross margins and percentages: 2023 total gross margin was $169.1 billion (44.1%), with Products at $108.8 billion (36.5%) and Services at $60.3 billion (70.8%). Product margin dollars declined due to currency weakness and lower volume, partly offset by savings and mix; its percentage rose due to savings and mix, partly offset by currency weakness and reduced leverage. Services margin dollars rose with sales, partly offset by currency weakness and costs; its percentage fell due to costs and currency, partly offset by mix. Apple warns gross margins face volatility and downward pressure. Operating expenses were $54.8 billion in 2023: R&D of $29.9 billion, up 14% mainly from headcount-related costs, and SG&A of $24.9 billion, roughly flat.

nodes.title: Gross Margins and Operating Expenses
nodes.summary: The page reports gross margins and margin percentages for Products and Services for 2023, 2022, and 2021. In 2023, Products gross margin fell year over year due to foreign currency weakness and lower volume, partly offset by cost savings and mix; its margin percentage rose as savings and mix outweighed currency weakness and reduced leverage. Services gross margin increased on higher net sales, partly offset by currency weakness and higher costs, while its margin percentage declined due to costs and currency, partly offset by mix. The company warns that gross margins may be volatile and face downward pressure. Operating expense figures and sales percentages are provided for 2023–2021: R&D rose in 2023, primarily from headcount-related expenses, while selling, general and administrative expense was relatively flat.

summary: Reports 2023 results and launches, including net sales of $383.3 billion and net income of $97.0 billion; sales declined 3% amid currency weakness and lower Mac and iPhone sales, partly offset by Services growth. It reviews product, software and service launches; share repurchases, dividends and macroeconomic risks; and regional and product-category sales for 2021–2023, including the drivers of changes. It also covers gross margins and percentages for Products and Services, factors affecting them and margin risks, plus operating expenses: R&D rose mainly with headcount-related costs, while SG&A was roughly flat.

title: Operating Expenses
summary: For 2023, total gross margin was $169.1 billion (44.1%), versus $170.8 billion (43.3%) in 2022 and $152.8 billion (41.8%) in 2021. Products margin fell in 2023 due to currency weakness and lower volume, partly offset by savings and mix; its percentage rose as savings and mix outweighed currency weakness and reduced leverage. Services margin increased on higher sales, partly offset by currency weakness and costs, while its percentage declined due to costs and currency, partly offset by mix. Gross margins may remain volatile and face downward pressure. Operating expenses rose 7% to $54.8 billion in 2023: R&D increased 14% to $29.9 billion, primarily from headcount-related expenses, while SG&A was nearly flat at $24.9 billion. Income tax provision was $16.7 billion, with a 14.7% effective rate, compared with $19.3 billion and 13.3% in 2022 and $14.5 billion and 16.2% in 2021; the statutory rate was 21% each year. Effective rates were below statutory mainly due to foreign earnings, the U.S. R&D credit, and share-based compensation benefits, partly offset by state taxes. The 2023 rate fell from 2022 due mainly to foreign earnings and Treasury foreign tax credit regulations, partly offset by reduced share-based compensation benefits.

title: Liquidity and Capital Resources
key_items: Debt; Leases; Manufacturing Purchase Obligations; Other Purchase Obligations; Deemed Repatriation Tax Payable
summary: As of September 30, 2023, the Company held $148.3 billion in cash, cash equivalents and unrestricted marketable securities, and expects these resources, operating cash flow and debt-market access to cover cash needs and capital returns for at least 12 months. Obligations include $106.6 billion in fixed-rate debt ($9.9 billion due within 12 months) and $41.1 billion in related interest ($2.9 billion due), $6.0 billion in commercial paper, $15.8 billion in lease payments ($2.0 billion due), $53.1 billion in primarily noncancelable manufacturing commitments ($52.9 billion due), $21.9 billion in other purchase commitments ($5.6 billion due), and $22.0 billion in deemed repatriation tax ($6.5 billion due). The Company also has an authorized, non-mandatory share repurchase program and a $0.24 quarterly dividend, which it intends to increase annually subject to Board approval.

title: Critical Accounting Estimates
key_items: Uncertain Tax Positions; Legal and Other Contingencies
summary: Financial reporting under U.S. GAAP requires management judgments, assumptions, and estimates based on experience and reasonable assumptions to determine reported amounts and asset and liability carrying values; significant policies are detailed in Note 1. Uncertain tax positions across U.S. and foreign jurisdictions require judgment amid complex laws, and reserves may change as facts or examinations resolve; outcomes differing from expectations could materially affect results or financial condition. Legal claims are also uncertain; liabilities are recorded when loss is probable and estimable, with significant judgment, and unexpected outcomes could have similar material effects.

title: Market Risk and Interest Rate Exposure
key_items: Item 7A. Quantitative and Qualitative Disclosures About Market Risk
summary: The Company faces interest-rate and foreign-exchange risks that may affect its consolidated financial statements despite risk-management strategies. It is primarily exposed to U.S. interest-rate changes affecting its investment portfolio and term debt; rate increases lower portfolio fair value and raise debt interest expense. Mitigation may include derivatives, offsetting sensitive assets and liabilities, and managing portfolio duration. A table reports impacts of a 100-basis-point increase across all tenors: portfolio fair-value declines of $3,089 million in 2023 and $4,022 million in 2022, and annual term-debt interest-expense increases of $194 million and $201 million, respectively.

title: Foreign Exchange Rate Risk
summary: The Company faces foreign exchange risk because it receives currencies other than U.S. dollars; dollar strengthening can reduce reported sales and gross margins and exchange-rate changes can affect asset and liability fair values. It may hedge with derivatives, offset exposures, or adjust local pricing, but may leave exposures unhedged due to cost or accounting concerns. A Monte Carlo VAR model estimated 95%-confidence maximum one-day derivative fair-value losses of $669 million in 2023 and $1.0 billion in 2022; underlying exposures, excluded from the model, generally offset derivative-value changes. The text lists the 2023 Form 10-K financial statements, notes, and auditor reports, and explains that schedules were omitted because they were inapplicable, immaterial, or included elsewhere.

title: CONSOLIDATED STATEMENTS OF OPERATIONS
summary: Apple Inc.’s consolidated statements of operations compare fiscal years ended September 25, 2021, September 24, 2022, and September 30, 2023. They report product and services net sales; corresponding cost of sales; gross margin; research and development and selling, general and administrative expenses; operating income; other income or expense; pretax income; income tax provision; net income; basic and diluted earnings per share; and shares used to calculate those earnings. Amounts are in millions except share counts, in thousands, and per-share figures. The statements refer readers to the accompanying financial-statement notes.

title: CONSOLIDATED STATEMENTS OF COMPREHENSIVE INCOME
summary: Apple Inc.’s consolidated statements of comprehensive income (in millions) present net income for fiscal years ended September 24, 2022, September 30, 2023, and September 25, 2021, alongside other comprehensive income or loss: foreign-currency translation; unrealized derivative gains or losses, including fair-value changes and amounts realized in net income; and unrealized marketable-debt-security gains or losses, with the same breakdown. The statement reports total other comprehensive income or loss and total comprehensive income and refers readers to the accompanying financial-statement notes.

title: Apple Consolidated Balance Sheets
summary: Apple Inc.’s consolidated balance sheets compare assets, liabilities, and shareholders’ equity at September 30, 2023, and September 24, 2022, in millions (shares in thousands, except par value). They detail current and non-current assets; current and non-current liabilities; commitments and contingencies; and equity components, including common stock, accumulated deficit, and accumulated other comprehensive loss. The statements conclude with total assets and total liabilities and equity and refer readers to the accompanying notes.

title: CONSOLIDATED STATEMENTS OF SHAREHOLDERS’ EQUITY
summary: Apple’s consolidated statements of shareholders’ equity report, in millions, the annual changes for fiscal years 2021–2023 in total equity and its components: common stock and additional paid-in capital (issuances, withheld shares, and share-based compensation); retained earnings/accumulated deficit (net income, declared dividends, withheld shares, and repurchases); and accumulated other comprehensive income or loss. Total ending equity was $63.090 billion in 2021, $50.672 billion in 2022, and $62.146 billion in 2023. Declared dividends per share or RSU were $0.85, $0.90, and $0.94, respectively. The statements refer readers to the accompanying financial-statement notes.

title: CONSOLIDATED STATEMENTS OF CASH FLOWS

nodes.title: CONSOLIDATED STATEMENTS OF CASH FLOWS (intro)
nodes.summary: Apple’s consolidated cash flow statements report operating, investing, and financing cash flows, cash balances, and supplemental cash paid for taxes and interest for fiscal years 2021–2023. The accompanying accounting policies explain the consolidated entities, use of GAAP estimates and reclassifications, fiscal-year timing, and methods for revenue, share-based compensation, cash equivalents, securities, inventories, property and equipment, derivatives, income taxes, and leases.

nodes.title: Summary of Significant Accounting Policies
nodes.summary: Apple’s consolidated financial statements include its wholly owned subsidiaries, use GAAP-based management estimates, and reclassify prior-period amounts when needed. Its fiscal year ends on the last Saturday of September and generally has 52 weeks, with a 53rd week in 2023. Revenue excludes taxes collected for authorities; share-based compensation is recognized straight-line for awards expected to vest. Cash equivalents mature within three months; securities sold use specific identification; inventories use FIFO; property and equipment depreciation is straight-line. Derivatives are reported at gross fair value, certain deferred taxes relate to the foreign-earnings minimum tax, and lease and nonlease components are combined for specified facilities.

nodes.title: Note 2 – Revenue
nodes.summary: Revenue is recognized when control transfers: generally upon shipment for products and over time as services are delivered; expected returns and customer incentives reduce product sales. For distinct obligations, revenue and discounts are allocated using observable or estimated stand-alone selling prices. Device sales may include hardware/software, bundled services, and future software upgrades; hardware revenue is recognized at shipment, while bundled services and upgrades are deferred and recognized over their expected delivery period. Unbilled, undelivered long-term services are not recognized. Third-party sales are reported gross when Apple controls the product before transfer, but App Store application commissions are reported net. The note reports 2021–2023 sales by product and service category, deferred-revenue amortization included in those sales, revenue recognized from prior-year deferred revenue, generally consistent segment sales mix except for a higher iPhone share in Greater China, and deferred revenue balances and expected recognition timing.

nodes.title: Note 3 – Earnings Per Share
nodes.summary: Note 3 reports Apple’s 2021–2023 basic and diluted EPS calculations, including net income, weighted-average shares and dilutive awards; about 24 million RSUs were excluded in 2023 as antidilutive. Note 4 details 2023 and 2022 cash, cash equivalents and marketable securities by investment type, fair-value level, valuation inputs and balance-sheet classification. It notes restricted securities of $13.8 billion and $12.7 billion, respectively, and gives 2023 non-current debt securities’ fair values by maturity. Debt securities are available-for-sale and classified current or non-current by contractual maturity.

nodes.title: Derivative Instruments and Hedging
nodes.summary: The Company uses derivatives to partially hedge foreign-exchange and interest-rate risks, though it may leave exposures unhedged and hedges may be incomplete; related cash flows generally follow the hedged items’ operating classification. Instruments include forwards, options, swaps and other contracts, designated as cash-flow or fair-value hedges or left undesignated. Foreign-exchange hedges cover forecast revenue and inventory (typically up to 12 months), debt and securities (up to 19 years for specified debt exposures), and remeasurement gains or losses; interest-rate hedges protect debt and securities. The text reports 2023 and 2022 derivative notionals, 2022 gross derivative fair values and balance-sheet classification, Level 2 valuation, and credit protections through collateral and netting (reducing assets and liabilities by $7.8 billion to a $412 million net asset). It also introduces carrying amounts of assets and liabilities hedged in fair-value hedges.

nodes.title: Accounts Receivable
nodes.summary: The text reports Apple’s trade receivables and customer credit concentration, including cellular carriers’ shares and credit support practices, plus vendor non-trade receivables, their accounting treatment, and concentration among major vendors. It presents 2023 and 2022 property and equipment by asset class, accumulated depreciation, net totals, and depreciation expense for 2021–2023. It also lists other non-current assets and current and non-current liabilities for 2023 and 2022, and details other income and expense—including interest and dividend income, interest expense, and other items—for 2021–2023.

nodes.title: Property, Plant and Liability Details
nodes.summary: Note 5 reports property, plant and equipment by asset class, accumulated depreciation, net balances for 2023 and 2022, and depreciation expense for 2023, 2022 and 2021. Note 6 introduces consolidated financial statement details for 2023 and 2022, listing deferred tax assets and other non-current assets; income taxes payable and other current liabilities; and long-term taxes payable and other non-current liabilities.

nodes.title: Other Income/(Expense), Net
nodes.summary: The text reports Apple’s other income and expense, including interest and dividend income, interest expense, and net totals for 2021–2023. It details income-tax provisions by federal, state, and foreign current and deferred taxes, foreign pretax earnings, and reconciliations to the 21% statutory rate, including effective tax rates. It also lists 2022–2023 deferred tax assets and liabilities, net deferred tax assets, and indefinite foreign tax and California R&D credit carryforwards, with valuation allowances.

nodes.title: Uncertain Tax Positions
nodes.summary: At September 30, 2023, Apple reported $19.5 billion in gross unrecognized tax benefits, of which $9.5 billion would affect its effective tax rate, compared with $16.8 billion and $8.0 billion, respectively, in 2022. The text details annual changes in these balances for 2021–2023, excluding interest and penalties. Apple files in U.S. federal, state, and foreign jurisdictions; federal tax years after 2017 and certain major foreign years after 2014 remain open to examination. Benefits may decrease by up to $4.5 billion within 12 months.

nodes.title: European Commission State Aid Decision
nodes.summary: The European Commission’s 2016 State Aid Decision found Ireland granted the Company unlawful aid through 1991 and 2007 tax opinions and ordered recovery of additional taxes for June 2003–December 2014. The €13.1 billion recovery, plus €1.2 billion interest, was appealed by the Company and Ireland; the General Court annulled the decision in 2020, and the Commission appealed. Following a May 2023 hearing, an ECJ decision was expected in 2024. The Company may claim U.S. foreign tax credits on some potential Irish taxes. Ireland may approve annual reductions for taxes paid elsewhere; as of September 30, 2023, the adjusted recovery was €12.7 billion excluding interest. The amount plus interest is held in restricted escrow pending the legal outcome.

nodes.title: Note 8 – Leases
nodes.summary: Note 8 describes leases for equipment and corporate, data center, manufacturing and retail facilities, generally with terms up to 10 years and renewal options. It reports fixed and variable lease costs, operating-lease cash payments and noncash right-of-use asset additions for 2021–2023; operating and finance ROU assets and liabilities and their balance-sheet classifications for 2022–2023; and 2023 lease-liability maturities, including undiscounted payments and imputed interest. It also gives weighted-average lease terms and discount rates for 2022–2023, and $544 million in uncommenced future lease payments, primarily for facilities and retail space, beginning in 2024–2026 with terms of 1–21 years. The excerpt then begins Note 9, Debt.

nodes.title: Commercial Paper
nodes.summary: The Company’s commercial paper program issues unsecured short-term notes for general corporate purposes, including dividends and share repurchases. Outstanding balances were $6.0 billion in 2023 and $10.0 billion in 2022, generally maturing within nine months, at weighted-average rates of 5.28% and 2.31%; issuance and repayment cash flows are reported for 2021–2023. Term debt comprises senior unsecured Notes with interest payable in arrears: principal totaled $106.6 billion in 2023 versus $111.8 billion in 2022, with issuance details, effective rates, adjustments, current and non-current portions, and future principal payments disclosed. Swaps manage interest-rate and foreign-exchange risks. Term-debt interest expense was $3.7 billion, $2.8 billion, and $2.6 billion in 2023, 2022, and 2021; fair values were $90.8 billion and $98.8 billion in 2023 and 2022.

nodes.title: Share Repurchase Program
nodes.summary: In 2023, Apple repurchased 471 million shares for $76.6 billion, excluding applicable excise tax; its programs require no minimum purchases and allow negotiated or open-market transactions, including Rule 10b5-1 plans. The text reports common-stock share counts and changes from 2021–2023. It also describes the shareholder-approved 2022 Employee Stock Plan, its eligible equity awards, typical four-year vesting and one-for-one share settlement of RSUs, dividend equivalent rights, and authorization of about 1.3 billion shares.

nodes.title: 2014 Employee Stock Plan
nodes.summary: Apple’s shareholder-approved 2014 Employee Stock Plan provided broad-based equity grants to employees, including executives, and allowed substantially the same equity awards and terms as the 2022 Plan, as well as cash bonus awards. The Company ended authority to grant new awards under the plan in the third quarter of 2022.

nodes.title: Restricted Stock Units
nodes.summary: The text reports Apple’s RSU activity for 2021–2023, including grants, vesting, cancellations, balances and fair values. It gives vested RSU fair values, shares withheld and tax remittances, share-based compensation expense and related tax benefits, and unrecognized RSU compensation cost and recognition period. It also summarizes future unconditional purchase obligations, management’s assessment of legal contingencies, risks from concentrated or constrained component supplies and custom parts, and the countries where outsourced hardware manufacturing primarily occurs.

nodes.title: Commitments, Contingencies and Supply Concentrations
key_items: Concentrations in the Available Sources of Supply of Materials and Product
nodes.summary: Reports share-based compensation expense and tax benefits for 2021–2023, plus $18.6 billion in unrecognized RSU compensation expected to be recognized over 2.5 years. Describes $20.736 billion in future unconditional purchase obligations, primarily for suppliers, licensed content and distribution rights. Notes legal claims are unresolved but management considers material losses not reasonably possible. Explains component sourcing risks, shortages, price fluctuations, custom-component and supplier-capacity constraints, and reliance on outsourcing partners mainly in Asia.

nodes.title: Note 13 – Segment Information and Geographic Data
nodes.summary: The note describes Apple’s five geographically managed reportable segments—Americas, Europe, Greater China, Japan, and Rest of Asia Pacific—their regional definitions, and how net sales and operating income are measured; segment asset information is not provided to the chief operating decision maker. It presents segment sales and operating income for 2021–2023, reconciles segment operating income to consolidated operating income through R&D and other corporate expenses, and identifies the U.S. and China as the only countries exceeding 10% of sales in those years. It also reports sales and long-lived assets by U.S., China (including Hong Kong and Taiwan), and other countries.

summary: Presents Apple’s 2021–2023 consolidated cash flows and significant accounting policies, then financial-statement notes covering revenue, EPS, cash and securities, derivatives, receivables, property and equipment, assets and liabilities, other income, income taxes and uncertain tax positions, and the European Commission State Aid case. It also details leases, commercial paper and debt, share repurchases and employee equity plans, RSUs, purchase commitments, legal and supply risks, and segment and geographic sales, operating income, and long-lived assets.

title: Report of Independent Registered Public Accounting Firm

nodes.title: Apple Independent Auditor’s Report
nodes.summary: The auditor gives an unqualified opinion that Apple’s 2023 and 2022 consolidated financial statements and three-year results conform to U.S. GAAP, and separately reports an unqualified opinion on internal control over financial reporting as of September 30, 2023. The report explains management’s and the auditor’s responsibilities, the auditor’s PCAOB independence and audit standards, and procedures supporting reasonable assurance. It defines critical audit matters and clarifies that they do not change or create a separate opinion; a matter description heading follows.

nodes.title: Uncertain Tax Positions
nodes.summary: Apple reported $19.5 billion in gross unrecognized tax benefits at September 30, 2023, of which $9.5 billion would affect its effective tax rate if recognized; evaluating these positions requires significant legal interpretation and judgment. EY tested related controls and assessed management’s analyses, tax-authority communications, technical merits, legal confirmations, and disclosures, using tax specialists and external advisers. EY, Apple’s auditor since 2009, also opined that internal control over financial reporting was effective in all material respects under COSO criteria. The report describes management’s and auditor’s responsibilities, audit procedures and reasonable-assurance basis, defines internal controls, and notes their inherent limitations and risks over time.

nodes.title: Apple Internal Control Audit Report
key_items: Opinion on Internal Control Over Financial Reporting
Definition and Limitations of Internal Control Over Financial Reporting
nodes.summary: Ernst & Young reports that Apple maintained effective internal control over financial reporting in all material respects as of September 30, 2023, and notes its separate unqualified opinion on Apple’s financial statements. The report explains management’s and the auditor’s responsibilities, PCAOB audit standards and procedures, and the basis for the opinion. It defines internal control’s purpose and key functions, while noting that controls may not prevent or detect misstatements and that effectiveness may change over time. Signed in San Jose on November 2, 2023.

nodes.title: Accounting Changes and Internal Control Assessment
key_items: Item 9. Changes in and Disagreements with Accountants on Accounting and Financial Disclosure
Evaluation of Disclosure Controls and Procedures
Management’s Annual Report on Internal Control over Financial Reporting
nodes.summary: The company reports no changes or disagreements with its accountants. Management found disclosure controls effective as of September 30, 2023. The text describes internal controls’ purposes and limitations, noting they provide reasonable but not absolute assurance and may weaken with changing conditions or reduced compliance. Management assessed financial reporting controls under the 2013 COSO framework and found them effective as of that date; Ernst & Young issued an audit report included in Part II, Item 8.

nodes.title: Changes in Internal Control over Financial Reporting
nodes.summary: Apple reported no fourth-quarter 2023 changes to internal control over financial reporting that materially affected or were likely to materially affect it. On August 30, 2023, executives Deirdre O’Brien and Jeff Williams adopted Rule 10b5-1 plans to sell shares vesting under specified equity awards, excluding shares withheld for taxes; the plans expire October 15 and December 15, 2024, respectively, subject to specified early termination. Foreign-jurisdiction inspection disclosure is not applicable. Required information on directors and governance, executive compensation, ownership and stockholder matters, related transactions and director independence, and auditor fees and services will appear in the 2024 Proxy Statement and is incorporated by reference.

nodes.title: Insider Trading and Part III Disclosures
key_items: Insider Trading Arrangements; Item 9C. Disclosure Regarding Foreign Jurisdictions that Prevent Inspections
Item 9C. Disclosure Regarding Foreign Jurisdictions that Prevent Inspections
Item 10. Directors, Executive Officers and Corporate Governance
Item 12. Security Ownership of Certain Beneficial Owners and Management and Related Stockholder Matters
Item 13. Certain Relationships and Related Transactions, and Director Independence
Item 14. Principal Accountant Fees and Services
nodes.summary: Reports that Deirdre O’Brien and Jeff Williams adopted Rule 10b5-1 trading plans on August 30, 2023, to sell vested award shares, excluding shares withheld for taxes; their plans expire October 15 and December 15, 2024, respectively, with specified early-termination provisions. Item 9C is not applicable. Part III disclosures on directors and governance, executive compensation, security ownership, related transactions and director independence, and accountant fees and services will appear in the 2024 proxy statement and are incorporated by reference.

nodes.title: PART IV
key_items: (3) Exhibits required by Item 601 of Regulation S-K (1)
nodes.summary: Part IV, Item 15 lists the report’s financial statements: consolidated operations, comprehensive income, balance sheets, shareholders’ equity, cash flows, notes, and the independent auditor’s reports for the specified years. Financial statement schedules are omitted as inapplicable, immaterial, or included elsewhere. The exhibit index covers corporate charter and bylaws, securities descriptions, debt indentures and note certificates, compensation and equity plans and award forms, subsidiaries, auditor consent, power of attorney, executive certifications, and Inline XBRL files. It identifies incorporation-by-reference details and exhibit filing designations, notes omitted debt instruments will be supplied to the SEC on request, and states that the Form 10-K summary is none.

summary: Reports unqualified opinions on Apple’s 2023 and 2022 financial statements and on the effectiveness of internal controls as of September 30, 2023. It explains management’s and the auditor’s responsibilities, audit standards, procedures, reasonable assurance, critical audit matters, and control limitations. It details the audit of uncertain tax positions, reports effective disclosure and financial-reporting controls and no material control changes, and describes executives’ Rule 10b5-1 plans. It notes certain required disclosures are incorporated from the 2024 proxy statement and lists Part IV financial statements, omitted schedules, exhibits, and the absence of a Form 10-K summary.

title: SIGNATURES
summary: Apple’s Form 10-K signatures section states that the report was authorized and signed for the company on November 2, 2023, by CFO Luca Maestri. It grants Timothy Cook and Luca Maestri joint and several power of attorney to sign and file amendments and related materials. It lists 11 signatories, their executive, accounting, or director roles—including principal executive, financial, and accounting officers—and notes that all signed on November 2, 2023.

title: DESCRIPTION OF THE REGISTRANT’S SECURITIES REGISTERED PURSUANT TO SECTION 12 OF THE SECURITIES EXCHANGE ACT OF 1934
summary: As of September 30, 2023, Apple had ten securities registered under Section 12 of the Exchange Act: common stock and nine note issues with stated interest rates and maturities from 2024 to 2042. All are listed on The Nasdaq Stock Market LLC.

title: DESCRIPTION OF COMMON STOCK
key_items: Dividends; Right to Receive Liquidation Distributions; No Preemptive or Similar Rights
Anti-Takeover Provisions of the Articles, Bylaws and California Law; Listing
Anti-Takeover Provisions of the Articles, Bylaws and California Law
summary: The text describes Apple common stock rights under its Articles, Bylaws, and California law. The Company is authorized to issue 50.4 billion shares; outstanding shares are fully paid and nonassessable. Each share has one vote, with no cumulative voting; it outlines approval thresholds, director elections and removal, vacancy filling, amendments, and meeting adjournments. Shareholders may receive board-declared dividends and pro rata liquidation distributions, but have no preemptive, conversion, redemption, or sinking-fund rights. Anti-takeover provisions cover director vacancies, advance notice, proxy access, and special meetings; California law requires a fairness opinion for certain interested-party reorganizations. Shares trade on Nasdaq as AAPL.

title: DESCRIPTION OF DEBT SECURITIES

nodes.title: The Notes
key_items: The 2024 Notes; The 0.000% 2025 Notes; The 0.875% 2025 Notes; The 2026 Notes; The 2027 Notes
The 1.375% 2029 Notes; The 3.050% 2029 Notes; The 2031 Notes; The 2042 Notes
nodes.summary: Apple’s Notes summary is qualified by its 2013 and 2018 Indentures with The Bank of New York Mellon Trust Company, governed by New York law. The Indentures impose no issuance limit and allow additional similar securities to join an existing series without holder consent, subject to ISIN conditions. As of October 20, 2023, the text lists outstanding principal, issue and maturity dates, interest rates, and payment schedules for nine euro- or sterling-denominated Note series maturing from 2024 to 2042.

nodes.title: Ranking
nodes.summary: The Notes rank equally with the issuer’s other senior unsecured, unsubordinated debt, but are structurally subordinated to subsidiary debt and preferred stock and effectively subordinated to secured debt up to the value of its collateral. Subsidiary creditors generally have priority over the issuer’s creditors, including Noteholders, regarding subsidiary assets and earnings. The Indentures do not limit the issuer or its subsidiaries from incurring additional debt.

nodes.title: Payment on the Notes
nodes.summary: The specified 2024–2031 euro-denominated notes are payable in euros, but payments switch to U.S. dollars if euros become unavailable or cease qualifying for use; conversion uses the Federal Reserve rate or, absent one, the latest Wall Street Journal rate before the second Business Day preceding payment. Such dollar payments are not defaults. Their Business Day definition requires New York and London banks to be open and TARGET2 operating. The 3.050% 2029 and 2042 notes are payable in pounds sterling, or euros if the UK adopts the euro, with similar dollar fallback, conversion, and no-default provisions. Their Business Day definition excludes bank holidays in New York, London, or the payment location.

nodes.title: Payment of Additional Amounts
nodes.summary: The Notes generally require principal and interest payments without U.S. tax withholding. The Company must pay non-U.S. holders Additional Amounts to preserve the stated net payment, subject to exceptions for U.S.-connected holders or entities, intermediary or beneficial-owner status, failures to provide required tax documentation, non-withholding taxes, late-effective legal changes, specified non-income taxes, alternative paying-agent availability, late presentation, FATCA-related taxes, and combinations of these exceptions. The Notes remain subject to applicable tax laws and interpretations, and the Company otherwise owes no tax payments. The text defines “United States” and “United States person” for these provisions and tax-redemption provisions.

nodes.title: Redemption for Tax Reasons
nodes.summary: The issuer may redeem an entire Notes series, but not part of it, if qualifying U.S. tax-law or official-interpretation changes announced or effective on or after the applicable prospectus supplement date cause, or counsel says will cause, additional-amounts obligations. Redemption requires 30–60 days’ notice for the 2024, 2026, 2027, 3.050% 2029, and 2042 Notes; 15–60 days for the 0.875% 2025 and 1.375% 2029 Notes; and 10–60 days for the 0.000% 2025 and 2031 Notes. The price is 100% of principal plus accrued unpaid interest through the redemption date, except interest for the last two series does not accrue through that date.

nodes.title: Optional Redemption
nodes.summary: The terms describe optional redemption prices and procedures. The 2024, 2026, 2027, 3.050% 2029 and 2042 Notes may be redeemed at any time at the greater of par or the present value of remaining payments, discounted at the applicable government-bond rate plus specified spreads. Before their Par Call Dates, the 0.000% and 0.875% 2025, 1.375% 2029 and 2031 Notes use a similar calculation assuming maturity at the Par Call Date, with specified spreads; on or after those dates, redemption is at par. Par Call Dates are three months before maturity. Accrued interest is paid through, but excluding, redemption; interest due on or before redemption remains payable to record-date holders. The text defines the comparable government bonds for each note group and the rate calculation, including its valuation date, market-price basis, rounding and independent-bank determination.

nodes.title: Covenants
key_items: Consolidation, Merger and Sale of Assets
nodes.summary: The Indentures contain limited covenants but do not restrict the amount of debt or lease obligations, secured debt, or dividends, distributions, and stock repurchases or redemptions. They permit mergers, consolidations, or transfers of substantially all assets if the successor is appropriately organized in the U.S., assumes the obligations and conversion rights, and no default continues; under the 2013 Indenture, the trustee must also receive an officers’ certificate and legal opinion. The successor replaces the issuer and assumes its rights and powers, while the issuer is released from obligations. “Person” is broadly defined to include individuals, entities, and governments.

nodes.title: Events of Default
nodes.summary: The text defines series-specific events of default: overdue interest (30 days), unpaid principal or premium, uncured covenant breaches after 90 days’ notice (with 2013/2018 holder thresholds of 25%/33%), specified voluntary or court-ordered insolvency events, and any additional series-specific defaults. It defines Bankruptcy Law and Custodian; explains acceleration, automatic acceleration for certain insolvency defaults, and majority-holder rescission. Defaults need not affect other series. The issuer must provide an annual officer’s compliance/default statement. Individual holders’ right to sue is subject to notice, holder-request, indemnity, and waiting-period conditions; majorities may direct remedies or waive certain defaults. The trustee’s duties and indemnity protections are described, while each holder retains an unconditional right to payment and to sue to enforce it.

nodes.title: Modification and Waivers
nodes.summary: Indenture amendments generally require consent from holders of a majority of the affected series, while changes to specified fundamental payment, redemption, currency, enforcement, voting, waiver, or conversion rights require each affected holder’s consent. The company and trustee may make listed changes without holder consent, including adding protections, defaults, guarantees, security, trustees or securities, adjusting forms and procedures, addressing series-specific provisions, curing defects, and making non-materially adverse or legally required changes. A majority of a series may waive certain covenants or past defaults, except payment defaults and provisions requiring unanimous consent; a waiver cures only the specified default, not later defaults.

nodes.title: Discharge, Defeasance and Covenant Defeasance
nodes.summary: The text explains discharge of Notes by depositing sufficient funds for near-term maturity or redemption, and legal or covenant defeasance through an irrevocable deposit of cash or qualifying government obligations. It notes surviving duties, payment sufficiency and acceleration risks, and country-specific German or UK obligations eligible for certain series. Defeasance requires a tax opinion; legal defeasance may follow covenant defeasance. Notes are held as global book-entry securities, with conditional exchange into specified euro- or sterling-denominated certificates. The Bank of New York Mellon Trust Company is trustee and also has banking, custodial, trustee and paying-agent relationships with the issuer.

nodes.title: Notes Settlement, Certificated Exchange, and Trustee
nodes.summary: Legal defeasance requires a tax opinion that holders and beneficial owners will not recognize federal taxable income, gain, or loss; for legal defeasance, the opinion must rely on an IRS ruling or change in law. It may be chosen after covenant defeasance. Notes are held in global book-entry form through Euroclear and Clearstream. Subject to specified depositary, issuer, or continuing-default events, global notes may be exchanged for definitive notes in stated euro or sterling denominations; otherwise, global notes are not exchangeable except for replacement global notes. BNYM is trustee and also has banking, custodial, trustee, and paying-agent relationships with the issuer.

summary: Describes the Notes’ governing indentures, outstanding series, ranking, payment currencies and fallback exchange rates, tax withholding and additional amounts, tax and optional redemption, and limited covenants. It covers defaults, acceleration, holder and trustee rights, amendments and waivers, discharge and defeasance, global book-entry settlement and exchange for definitive notes, and the trustee’s other relationships with Apple.

title: Subsidiaries of Apple Inc.*
summary: Exhibit 21.1 lists Apple Inc. subsidiaries and their jurisdictions of incorporation, including entities in Hong Kong, the U.S., Canada, China, Ireland, India, Japan, South Korea, Mexico, Australia, Thailand, and Vietnam. A note states that other subsidiary names are omitted under Regulation S-K Item 601(b)(21)(ii) because they are not significant subsidiaries in aggregate at year-end. The text also begins Exhibit 23.1.

title: Consent of Independent Registered Public Accounting Firm
summary: Ernst & Young consents to incorporating its November 2, 2023 reports on Apple’s consolidated financial statements and internal control effectiveness into seven specified S-3 and S-8 registration statements. Apple CEO Timothy Cook and CFO Luca Maestri each certify that they reviewed the 2023 Form 10-K, believe it contains no material misstatements or omissions and fairly presents financial results, and describe their responsibilities for disclosure controls and financial reporting controls, their evaluation and reporting of control changes, and disclosure of significant deficiencies, material weaknesses, and relevant fraud to auditors and the audit committee. Both certifications are dated November 2, 2023.

title: CERTIFICATIONS OF CHIEF EXECUTIVE OFFICER AND CHIEF FINANCIAL OFFICER PURSUANT TO 18 U.S.C. SECTION 1350, AS ADOPTED PURSUANT TO SECTION 906 OF THE SARBANES-OXLEY ACT OF 2002
summary: Apple CEO Timothy D. Cook and CFO Luca Maestri certify, dated November 2, 2023, under Sarbanes-Oxley Act Section 906, that Apple’s fiscal 2023 Form 10-K complies with relevant Securities Exchange Act reporting requirements and fairly presents the company’s financial condition and operating results. Apple retains the signed original and will provide it to the SEC or its staff upon request.
